full_judgment:
12. The prosecution is not bound to produce a witness if he is not expected to give true evidence even though he may have been mentioned in the charge-sheet or F.I.R. If a prosecutor considers that a witness would depose falsely there would be justification for not examining him. If the prosecution collected all material witnesses and named them in the charge-sheet and examined sonic of them and did not examine the remaining charge-sheeted witnesses, in our view, no adverse presumption should be drawn in the case. 

 14. It has been suggested by the defence that since no blood stained earth was found or recovered from the place of occurrence and that no wound having been found on the body of the deceased or that any trail of blood leading to the house of the deceased could be found and recovered, a legitimate inference should be drawn that Israil Mia has been killed elsewhere. It has also been argued by the learned Advocate for the appellant that absence of any mud stain on the body of the deceased either in the inquest report or in the Post-mortem report would also lend a credence to the defence case that the occurrence did not take place in the field as alleged by the prosecution. According to the learned Advocate, if Israil fell down on the ground, his head downward, and the deceased was severely dealt with blows by sulfi, Jhata and dao, his body and wearing apparel would be stained and besmeared with mud, since the earth would be muddy and wet in the month of Bhadra. We are also of the view that if Israil fell down on ground, after he suffered the first three injuries, as deposed by P.Ws.1 to 3, his body and wearing apparel would be stained with blood. In the inquest report we do not finding anything that the officer who held the inquest report noticed any mud or blood on the body or wearing apparel of the deceased. It is also seen that no cloth or wearing apparel of the deceased was seized to show that it was stained or soaked with mud and blood. 15. The learned Advocate for the appellants has further submitted that no clothes of the persons who carried the dead-body of Israil from the alleged P.O. to the house were seized to examine whether their clothes were stained with blood while they carried the dead body from the P.O. to the house. He has also sub-witted that no blood stained earth from the house of the deceased, where Israil was taken from the alleged P.O. was seized by the Police to show that the deceased was taken to the house. The learned Advocate has submitted that in the absence of these material exhibits or alamats an adverse presumption against the prosecution is bound to arise. In this regards the learned Asstt. Attorney General has frankly submitted that the Police Officers who had done the inquest of the dead body and made the investigation were negligent in their duties and that they ought to have seized the wearing apparel of the deceased. the clothes of the persons who carried the dead-body from the alleged P.O. and the mud from the house of the deceased which must have been stained with blood of the deceased but the Police Officers acted in a negligent manner and did not collect these material evidences or alamats to prove the guilt of the accused appellants. He has also submitted that the Police ought to have seized the wearing apparel of the deceased. In this view absence of these material alamats, in our opinion, has strengthened the suggestion of the defence that Israil had been killed at a place different from that as has been alleged by the prosecution. 

 It is curious to note from his deposition that he has not seen the inflicting of the subsequent six injuries alleged to have been inflicted by the accused persons after Israil feel down on the ground. This witness has seen that the accused persons inflicted the three injuries and then they went away. This is clearly a departure from the prosecution case and amounted to a contradiction of the case of the prosecution that after Israil fell down the accused persons dealt six other serious injuries upon Israil. In view of this omission to depose on material facts which the witness would have done if he was present there, the natural presumption would be that he was not present at the P.O. and has not seen the occurrence. In view of the evidence of P.W.4 we are constrained to hold that this witness was not present at the place of occurrence and he has not seen the inflicting of injuries by the accused persons as alleged. We are thus left with two witnesses namely P.Ws.1 and 2 in support of the prosecution case. P.W. 1 is the son and P.W.2 is the wife respectively of the deceased, and upon their testimony alone we are not inclined to maintain the conviction of the appellants. To the facts of the case the conviction of the appellants should not be grounded upon the evidences of these two witnesses alone.
